query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be accurately predicted using a machine learning approach that incorporates explainable models, which can overcome the limitations of traditional analytical predictions and account for the effects of defects and oxygen contamination.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr with varying oxygen concentrations (0-1 wt.%)
generation.intervention: Introduction of oxygen contamination and defects
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of oxide scales and intermetallic phases
generation.mechanism: Oxygen contamination and defects affect the formation of oxide scales and intermetallic phases, which in turn influence the conductivity of the material
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved accuracy in predicting conductivity compared to traditional analytical approaches
generation.baseline: Conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr without oxygen contamination and defects
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 0-200 K and 300-1200 K; oxygen concentration: 0-1 wt.%
generation.uncertainty: Limited understanding of the effects of oxygen contamination and defects on the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr with varying oxygen concentrations (0-1 wt.%) at different temperatures (0-200 K and 300-1200 K)
measurements: Microstructural analysis using SEM and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted conductivity values do not match the experimental values within a certain margin of error (e.g. 10%), the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The Ti-rich oxides formed on the alloys ZX3 and ZX7 at 1200 °C are compared in the Table S14 in the Supplemental data. Ti-rich oxide was not found in the scales formed at 800 °C and also was not found in the scale formed on the alloy ZX5 at 1200 °C, which would suggest that Cr promoted the formation of this oxide only at 1200 °C. The average oxygen concentration in the oxides was close to that in NbO2 (66.7 at.%), TiO2 (66.7 at.%), and Nb2O5 (71.4 at.%) and could be considered to be mixtures of TiO2 and TiNb2O7 oxides []. The latter oxides have been identified in the scales formed on Nb-silicide-based alloys [,,]. The concentrations of elements in the oxide formed on the alloy ZX7 at 1200 °C were similar to those reported for the same oxide for the alloy JG6 at the same temperature []. The Sn concentration and the Nb + Ti sum were the same in the alloys ZX3 and ZX7.

The structure of the paper is as follows. First the approach used to design and select the two alloys is explained. Then the experimental techniques used for the characterisation of the alloys are described. The results for the cast and heat treated alloys are presented before their isothermal oxidation at 800 and 1200 °C is presented. The discussion considers first the macrosegregation and microstructures of the alloys, which are also compared with High Entropy Alloys, and then their oxidation behaviour is considered.

To date, the alloying elements that have been considered by our group for possible BC alloys are Al, Cr, Fe, Hf, Nb, Si, and Ti [,,,] and the alloying with Fe has been identified as not desirable owing to concerns about liquation []. The remaining elements are all known to improve the oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide-based alloys []. Two more elements are known to improve the oxidation of the latter alloys, namely B and Ge, owing to their effects on phase selection and stability [,,,]. Furthermore, when the alloying behaviour of Nb-silicide-based alloys is considered, the B-containing alloys form their own group []. It is important for future research to find out how B or Ge would affect the oxidation of BC alloys and the location of such alloys in maps of the parameters δ, Δχ, and VEC.
